# Biases of AI as a Judge

Like human evaluators, AI judges carry systematic biases that distort their scores independent of actual response quality. The book describes three recurring kinds.

**Self-bias**: a model favors its own responses over responses generated by other models, because the same mechanism that makes a response likely for the model to generate also causes that model to score it highly. In Zheng et al.'s (2023) experiment, [[gpt-4|GPT-4]] favored itself with a 10% higher win rate, while Claude-v1 favored itself with a 25% higher win rate (AIE p.144).

**First-position bias**: a judge may favor whichever answer appears first in a pairwise comparison or list of options. This is the opposite of the recency bias humans show (favoring the last-seen answer), and can be mitigated by repeating the same test with different answer orderings or with carefully crafted prompts (AIE p.144).

**Verbosity bias**: a judge favors lengthier answers regardless of quality. Wu and Aji (2023) found GPT-4 and Claude-1 both preferred longer responses (~100 words) containing factual errors over shorter, correct responses (~50 words). Saito et al. (2023) found that when one response is roughly twice as long as another, the judge almost always prefers the longer one, though GPT-4 was found less prone to this bias than GPT-3.5, suggesting it may lessen as models improve. Humans show a similar but much weaker preference for longer responses (Saito et al., 2023) (AIE p.144-145).

Beyond scoring biases, AI judges share the same privacy and IP limitations as any AI application: using a proprietary model as judge requires sending it your data, and an undisclosed training set means you cannot confirm the judge is commercially safe to use (AIE p.145).

## Key figures
- GPT-4 favors its own responses with a 10% higher win rate; Claude-v1 favors its own with a 25% higher win rate (Zheng et al., 2023) (AIE p.144)
- Judges preferred longer, factually flawed ~100-word responses over correct ~50-word responses (Wu and Aji, 2023) (AIE p.144)
